title: Special Relativity — Space, Time, and Light
description: Why the speed of light is constant and what it means for space and time

concepts.title: The Two Postulates
concepts.contentHtml:
Einstein's 1905 paper rests on two postulates:

1. The Principle of Relativity: The laws of physics are the same in all inertial (non-accelerating) reference frames. There is no absolute rest — only relative motion matters.

2. The Constancy of Light Speed: Light travels at c = 3 × 10⁸ m/s in vacuum in all inertial frames, regardless of the motion of the source or observer.

The second postulate seems absurd — if you run toward a beam of light, shouldn't it approach faster? No. It always clocks in at c. This forces space and time to be relative quantities.

concepts.title: Time Dilation
concepts.contentHtml:
Because the speed of light is constant, moving clocks must run slow. If a clock moves at speed v relative to you, you observe it running slow by factor γ = 1/√(1 − v²/c²).

Δt′ = γΔt. The faster the motion, the slower the clock. At v = 0.866c, γ = 2 — the clock runs at half speed.

This is experimentally confirmed: muons created in the upper atmosphere by cosmic rays travel fast enough that time dilation extends their lifetimes sufficiently to reach sea level. GPS satellites must correct for this effect or navigation errors of ~10 km per day would accumulate.

concepts.title: Length Contraction and Simultaneity
concepts.contentHtml:
Moving objects are measured to be shorter along the direction of motion: L = L₀/γ. At v = 0.866c (γ = 2), a 1 m ruler appears 0.5 m long to a stationary observer.

Perhaps more surprising: simultaneity is relative. Two events that appear simultaneous in one frame may not be in another. There is no universal 'now' — what events are simultaneous depends on who's asking.

All these effects — time dilation, length contraction, relativity of simultaneity — follow mathematically from the Lorentz transformation, which replaces the Galilean transformation of classical mechanics.

title: Mass, Energy, and Spacetime
description: E = mc², relativistic momentum, and the geometry of spacetime

concepts.title: E = mc² and Mass-Energy Equivalence
concepts.contentHtml:
The most famous equation in physics: mass and energy are equivalent. A rest mass m contains energy E = mc². Even a small mass stores enormous energy — 1 gram of matter contains mc² = 9 × 10¹³ joules (equivalent to ~21 kilotons of TNT).

This explains why nuclear reactions release so much energy: fission and fusion convert a small fraction of mass (mass defect) into energy. The Sun converts ~4 million tonnes of mass into energy every second via nuclear fusion.

The full relativistic energy is E = γmc², and rest energy (v = 0) is E₀ = mc².

concepts.title: Relativistic Momentum
concepts.contentHtml:
In special relativity, momentum is p = γmv — multiplied by the Lorentz factor. As v → c, momentum → ∞. This is why no massive object can reach c: accelerating it further always requires more force, and the required force diverges as v approaches c.

The energy-momentum relation: E² = (pc)² + (mc²)². For photons (m = 0): E = pc. For a stationary particle (p = 0): E = mc². This single equation unifies rest energy, kinetic energy, and massless particles.

concepts.title: Minkowski Spacetime
concepts.contentHtml:
Minkowski (1908) showed that special relativity is most elegantly expressed as geometry in 4-dimensional spacetime. Space and time are not separate — they are woven into a single 4D fabric.

The spacetime interval ds² = −(c dt)² + dx² + dy² + dz² is invariant — all observers agree on it, even though they disagree on space and time separately. This is the relativistic analog of the Pythagorean theorem.

Events separated by ds² < 0 are 'timelike' (one can causally influence the other). Events with ds² > 0 are 'spacelike' (no causal link). Events with ds² = 0 are 'lightlike' — on the light cone.

title: General Relativity — Gravity as Geometry
description: How mass curves spacetime and gravity becomes geometry

concepts.title: The Equivalence Principle
concepts.contentHtml:
Einstein's crucial insight (1907, his 'happiest thought'): standing on Earth's surface feeling 1g of gravity is locally indistinguishable from accelerating at 9.8 m/s² in empty space. Gravity and acceleration are locally equivalent.

This means light must bend in gravitational fields — if light bends in an accelerating rocket, and acceleration = gravity, light must bend in gravity too. Eddington's 1919 eclipse expedition confirmed this: starlight passing near the Sun was deflected by about the amount GR predicted.

The equivalence principle implies that gravity cannot be a force in the usual sense — it must be a property of spacetime itself.

concepts.title: Curved Spacetime and the Einstein Field Equations
concepts.contentHtml:
General relativity: mass and energy curve spacetime; curved spacetime tells matter how to move. John Wheeler summarised: 'Spacetime tells matter how to move; matter tells spacetime how to curve.'

Einstein's field equations: G_μν = 8πG/c⁴ × T_μν. The left side (Einstein tensor G_μν) describes spacetime curvature. The right side (stress-energy tensor T_μν) describes matter and energy content.

These are 10 coupled, non-linear partial differential equations — extraordinarily difficult to solve. Schwarzschild found the first exact solution (1915, weeks after Einstein published) for a spherically symmetric mass.

concepts.title: Gravitational Time Dilation and Redshift
concepts.contentHtml:
Clocks run slower in stronger gravitational fields — gravitational time dilation. A clock on Earth's surface runs slower than one on a GPS satellite (which is at higher altitude, weaker gravity).

GPS must correct for both special relativistic time dilation (satellite moves fast, clock slows) and general relativistic time dilation (satellite is higher, clock speeds up). Net effect: GR wins, GPS clocks must be slowed by ~38 μs/day before launch.

Gravitational redshift: photons climbing out of a gravitational well lose energy — their frequency decreases (they redshift). Confirmed by Pound-Rebka experiment (1959) measuring gamma ray redshift over a 22.5 m height difference.

title: Black Holes
description: What happens when gravity wins — and what lies beyond the event horizon

concepts.title: The Schwarzschild Radius and Event Horizon
concepts.contentHtml:
A black hole forms when mass is compressed inside its Schwarzschild radius r_s = 2GM/c². For Earth, r_s ≈ 9 mm. For the Sun, r_s ≈ 3 km.

The event horizon at r = r_s is a one-way membrane: anything crossing it cannot return. The escape velocity equals c at r_s — even light cannot escape.

The density needed to form a black hole decreases with mass. A supermassive black hole (10⁹ solar masses) has lower average density than water at its Schwarzschild radius — the key is total mass, not crushing pressure.

concepts.title: Spaghettification and Tidal Forces
concepts.contentHtml:
Near a black hole, tidal forces — gravity pulling harder on your feet than your head — become extreme. This spaghettification stretches any infalling object radially and squeezes it transversely.

For stellar-mass black holes (3–20 solar masses), spaghettification begins well outside the event horizon. For supermassive black holes (millions–billions of solar masses), you could cross the event horizon without noticing — tidal forces are gentle at the horizon because the horizon is so far from the singularity.

From an outside observer's view, an infalling clock slows infinitely at the horizon — they never see the object cross. From the infaller's view, they cross quickly and reach the singularity in finite proper time.

concepts.title: Observational Evidence
concepts.contentHtml:
Black holes are no longer hypothetical. Evidence includes:

— Stellar orbits: Stars at the Galactic Centre orbit an invisible mass of 4 million solar masses (Sagittarius A*). Genzel and Ghez won the 2020 Nobel Prize for this work.
— Gravitational waves: LIGO detected two merging black holes in 2015 — the first direct gravitational wave detection (Nobel 2017).
— Event Horizon Telescope: The 2019 image of M87*'s shadow and 2022 image of Sgr A* are direct visual evidence of event horizons.

title: Gravitational Waves and Cosmological Spacetime
description: Ripples in spacetime, expanding universe, and the frontiers of GR

concepts.title: Gravitational Waves
concepts.contentHtml:
Accelerating masses create ripples in spacetime — gravitational waves — predicted by Einstein in 1916, detected 100 years later by LIGO in 2015.

The first detection (GW150914) was from two black holes merging: 29 and 36 solar masses, 1.3 billion light-years away. The signal: spacetime stretching and squeezing by ~10⁻²¹ — a fraction of a proton's width over a 4 km detector arm.

Gravitational waves carry energy. Binary pulsar PSR 1913+16 (Hulse-Taylor, Nobel 1993) loses energy exactly as GR predicts from gravitational wave emission — indirect confirmation before LIGO.

concepts.title: Expanding Universe and the FLRW Metric
concepts.contentHtml:
On cosmological scales, spacetime itself is expanding. The Friedmann-Lemaître-Robertson-Walker (FLRW) metric describes a homogeneous, isotropic expanding universe: ds² = −c²dt² + a(t)²[dr²/(1−kr²) + r²dΩ²].

The scale factor a(t) describes how distances grow. Hubble's 1929 observation that galaxies recede at speeds proportional to distance (v = H₀d) was the first evidence of expansion. The Big Bang was not an explosion in space — it was an expansion of space itself.

The cosmological constant Λ, Einstein's 'greatest blunder' (introduced to make a static universe), turns out to be real — it drives the accelerating expansion discovered in 1998.

concepts.title: Open Problems: Singularities and Quantum Gravity
concepts.contentHtml:
GR predicts its own breakdown. At the Big Bang and inside black holes, curvature diverges to infinity — singularities. GR fails at these points; quantum effects must dominate.

The Penrose-Hawking singularity theorems (Penrose, Nobel 2020) prove that singularities are inevitable under general conditions — not just idealised symmetry. This makes quantum gravity not optional but mandatory.

Gravitational wave astronomy is a new window: multi-messenger events (GW170817 — neutron star merger seen in GW and light simultaneously) are probing GR in extreme conditions. Future detectors (LISA, Einstein Telescope) will probe the early universe and extreme spacetimes at unprecedented sensitivity.

concepts.title: Relativistic Energy and Momentum
concepts.contentHtml:
At low speeds, momentum is mv and kinetic energy is ½mv². At high speeds these break down.

The correct relativistic formulas: p = γmv, E = γmc², where γ = 1/√(1−v²/c²) is the Lorentz factor. As v → c, γ → ∞: infinite energy required to reach c.

The energy-momentum relation E² = (pc)² + (mc²)² holds in every frame. For a massless particle (photon), E = pc; for a particle at rest, E = mc² — Einstein's famous equation.

concepts.title: Particle Accelerators
concepts.contentHtml:
Particle accelerators routinely push electrons and protons to within a hair's breadth of c. At LHC energies, protons reach γ ≈ 7000 — they're effectively 'frozen' in space (length-contracted) and aging at 1/7000 the rate of lab clocks.

To create heavy particles like the Higgs (125 GeV) or top quark (173 GeV), you need at least that much energy concentrated in collisions. E = mc² makes these heavy creations possible — but only at relativistic energies.

concepts.title: Relativistic Doppler Effect
concepts.contentHtml:
For light, the relativistic Doppler shift is f_obs = f_emit · √((1−β)/(1+β)) for a source receding at speed βc.

This is what cosmologists use to measure recession velocities of galaxies via redshift. A galaxy with z = 1 (wavelengths doubled) is receding at about 0.6c.

The transverse Doppler effect — a clock moving past you at relativistic speed appears to run slow even when its instantaneous distance isn't changing — is purely relativistic. Confirmed experimentally with rapidly orbiting atoms.

concepts.title: Light Bends Around Mass
concepts.contentHtml:
GR predicts that mass curves spacetime, and light follows null geodesics through that curved spacetime. Around a massive object, geodesics bend.

Eddington's 1919 expedition measured starlight bending near the Sun during a total solar eclipse — the first major confirmation of GR. The deflection angle for light grazing the Sun is about 1.75 arcseconds.

Galaxy clusters and dark matter halos lens distant galaxies far more dramatically — multiple images, arcs, complete Einstein rings.

concepts.title: Strong vs Weak Lensing
concepts.contentHtml:
Strong lensing happens when a massive cluster lies near the line of sight to a background galaxy — multiple images, arcs, or rings appear.

Weak lensing is a subtle distortion of background galaxies by foreground mass — measured statistically over many galaxies. Weak lensing surveys (DES, Euclid, LSST) map the dark matter distribution of the universe.

Microlensing — temporary brightening when a small mass passes in front of a star — is used to detect exoplanets and probe stellar populations.

concepts.title: Probing Dark Matter
concepts.contentHtml:
Lensing is the cleanest probe of mass distribution: it doesn't care whether the mass is luminous or dark, hot or cold. The Bullet Cluster's lensing signature, offset from its X-ray-emitting hot gas, is the strongest evidence that dark matter is real (and not a modification of gravity).

Lensing also tests GR itself in the strong-field regime. Black hole shadows, captured by the Event Horizon Telescope, are gravitational lensing in extremis.

title: Relativity in Practice
description: Where you encounter relativity in daily life

concepts.title: GPS Time Corrections
concepts.contentHtml:
GPS satellites orbit at ~20,000 km altitude moving at ~14,000 km/h. Two relativistic effects on their clocks:

Special relativity: motion makes the clocks run slow by ~7 μs/day.
General relativity: weaker gravity at altitude makes clocks run fast by ~45 μs/day.

Net: GPS clocks run +38 μs/day faster than ground clocks. Without correction, position fixes would drift ~10 km per day. Every cellphone implicitly uses Einstein's relativity.

concepts.title: Muon Survival
concepts.contentHtml:
Cosmic-ray muons created in the upper atmosphere should decay (mean lifetime 2.2 μs) long before reaching the ground. They don't — many arrive intact.

From our frame, time dilation extends their lifetime; from the muon's frame, length contraction shortens the atmosphere. Either way, the calculation matches observation.

This was one of the first direct experimental tests of special relativity. Today, particle physicists routinely produce relativistic muons with γ ≈ 100, surviving long enough for slow-motion experiments.

concepts.title: Cosmic Time Dilation
concepts.contentHtml:
Distant supernovae appear to fade slower than nearby ones — by exactly the factor (1+z) that GR predicts. Not slower because they're farther; slower because their clocks are running slower from our cosmological frame.

This is one of the cleanest tests of cosmological time dilation. Confirmed observationally with hundreds of Type Ia supernovae.

Relativity isn't a curiosity — it's a routine, measurable effect in everyday astrophysics and engineering.
